title: M&A sell-side deal walk
description: Six multiple-choice stages following a sell-side M&A process.

concepts.name: Sell-side process
concepts.summary: The structured sequence a seller and its advisers run to market a company, collect bids and sign a sale, usually in two rounds.

concepts.name: Non-disclosure agreement
concepts.summary: A confidentiality agreement a prospective buyer signs before receiving non-public information about the target.

concepts.name: Confidential information memorandum
concepts.summary: The detailed marketing document (CIM) describing the business, market and financials, shared with buyers after they sign an NDA.

concepts.name: Indication of interest
concepts.summary: A non-binding first-round bid giving a valuation range and key assumptions, used to choose which buyers move forward.

concepts.name: Due diligence
concepts.summary: The buyer's detailed review of the target's business, financials, legal and other matters, usually through a virtual data room.

concepts.name: Purchase agreement
concepts.summary: The legal contract for the sale, covering price, representations, indemnities and conditions to closing.

concepts.name: Closing conditions
concepts.summary: Requirements, such as regulatory approvals, that must be satisfied before a signed deal can close.

multipleChoice.title: First steps of a sale
multipleChoice.prompt: A private company has decided to sell itself and hires an investment bank. Which work normally comes first, before any buyer is contacted?

options.text: Sending the confidential information memorandum to every potential buyer
Agreeing the engagement, then preparing valuation analysis, a teaser, the information memorandum and a list of potential buyers
Asking bidders to submit final binding offers
Signing the purchase agreement with the most likely buyer

explanation: A sale starts with preparation. The bank is engaged, analyses the company's value, and builds the marketing materials: a short anonymous teaser, the detailed information memorandum and a buyer list.
Only once these are ready does outreach begin. Offers and contracts come much later.

multipleChoice.title: Teaser and confidentiality
multipleChoice.prompt: The bank sends an anonymous teaser to potential buyers and one of them wants to read the detailed information memorandum. What must it normally do first?

options.text: Submit a binding offer
Complete full due diligence
Sign a non-disclosure agreement
Pay a deposit to the seller

explanation: The teaser is a short summary that does not name the company. Confidential details, including the information memorandum, are shared only after the buyer signs a non-disclosure agreement.
Binding offers and full diligence come much later, after the buyer has seen the memorandum.

multipleChoice.title: First-round bids
multipleChoice.prompt: After reading the information memorandum, interested buyers submit first-round indications of interest. What are these typically?

options.text: Legally binding offers that the seller must accept
The signed purchase agreement
Regulatory filings for the transaction
Non-binding indications of a valuation range and key assumptions

explanation: Indications of interest are non-binding. They give a price range and the main assumptions behind it, so the seller can decide which buyers to invite into the next round.
Binding offers come at the end of the process, after due diligence.

multipleChoice.title: Diligence and management meetings
multipleChoice.prompt: A shortlist of bidders moves into the second round. Which activity usually takes place in this stage?

options.text: Management presentations and access to a virtual data room for due diligence
Writing the teaser for the first time
Closing the transaction and transferring the shares
Choosing the investment bank to sell the company

explanation: Shortlisted bidders meet management and review detailed information, usually in a virtual data room, so they can confirm their valuation and prepare a final bid.
The teaser and bank selection happen earlier, and closing happens after signing.

multipleChoice.title: Final bids
multipleChoice.prompt: Final bids often come with a mark-up of the seller's draft purchase agreement. Why does the seller's bank ask for it?

options.text: Price is the only thing that matters once bids are final
So bids can be compared on terms such as indemnities, conditions and certainty of closing, not just price
Because the buyer's lawyers must write the information memorandum
It replaces the need for any due diligence

explanation: The highest headline price is not always the best bid. The mark-up shows what the buyer wants on indemnities, conditions and timing, which affects how likely the deal is to close and what the seller really receives.
It does not replace diligence, and the buyer does not write the seller's marketing materials.

multipleChoice.title: Signing and closing
multipleChoice.prompt: A purchase agreement is signed, but the deal needs regulatory approval. What is the usual order of events?

options.text: Closing happens first, and approvals are sought afterwards
Signing and closing always happen at the same moment
Approvals are requested only after the purchase price has been paid
Signing, then the closing conditions are satisfied, including approvals, then closing

explanation: When a deal needs approvals, signing and closing are separate. After signing, the parties work to satisfy the closing conditions, such as regulatory approvals, and the deal closes once they are met.
The price is normally paid at closing, not before the approvals.

processes.title: M&A sell-side process
processes.description: Follow a private company sale from preparing marketing materials through bids and diligence to signing and closing.
